Let $X$ be a Banach space. It has the **approximation property** (AP) if for

$$\sup_{x\in C}\|Tx-x\|<\varepsilon.$$

Here finite rank means that $T(X)$ is finite-dimensional.

For $\lambda\ge0$, $X$ has the **$\lambda$-bounded approximation property**

has the **bounded approximation property** (BAP) if it has $\lambda$-BAP for
some finite $\lambda$.

If $(u_n)$ is Cauchy in their norm, every derivative sequence has a uniform limit $g_\alpha$ on $\bar D$: pointwise real completeness gives the limit, and the uniform Cauchy estimate gives uniform convergence. Each $g_\alpha$ is continuous, since for a positive error one first approximates it uniformly by a fixed continuous $D^\alpha u_n$ and then applies continuity of that fixed function. Put $u=g_0$. Uniform convergence passes this identity to $g_\alpha(x+he_i)-g_\alpha(x)=\int_0^h g_{\alpha+e_i}(x+se_i)\,ds$, since the integral error is bounded by $|h|$ times the uniform error. By [F5], $\partial_i g_\alpha=g_{\alpha+e_i}$. Induction in $|\alpha|$ yields $D^\alpha u=g_\alpha$ in $D$ through order $m$, with the continuous extensions already supplied on $\bar D$. citations.quote: Let $d\ge2$, $0<\alpha\le1$, $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, and $\Gamma\subseteq\partial U$ be closed. Let $\mu_r$ and $\mu_b$ be probability measures with densities relative to $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure and $(d-1)$-dimensional Hausdorff measure. Assume each density is supported on the respective set and has a positive infimum. Assume that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there are partitions of $U$ and $\Gamma$ into cells contained in cubes of side $\varepsilon$, with cell masses at least $c_r\varepsilon^d$ and $c_b\varepsilon^{d-1}$, and that ball masses are at most $C_r\varepsilon^d$ and $C_b\varepsilon^{d-1}$, respectively. Let the residual and boundary samples be iid from these measures, with counts satisfying $m_r=O(m_b^{d/(d-1)})$ and $m_r,m_b\to\infty$ along nested iid sample sequences.

For $d\ge2$, $0<\alpha\le1$, and positive constants in equation (3.1), the count condition $m_r=O(m_b^{d/(d-1)})$ alone does not imply that the two threshold coordinates have bounded max-to-min ratio. In particular, choosing $\lambda_m^R=\widehat\lambda_m^R$ satisfies the stated coordinatewise lower bound and norm upper bound, while that ratio can diverge.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded, $T>0$, $Q=U\times(0,T)$, and $0<\alpha<1$. Let $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$ and $b_i$ be differentiable in space, and define
$$\widetilde b_i=\sum_{j=1}^dD_j a_{ij}+b_i+c_i,\qquad \widetilde c=\sum_{i=1}^dD_i b_i+d,\qquad \Omega=U\times(0,T).$$
Assume: (i) the minimum eigenvalue of $[a_{ij}(x,t)]$ is at least $\lambda_0>0$ on $\Omega$; (ii) $a_{ij},\widetilde b_i,\widetilde c$ are parabolic Hölder continuous of exponent $\alpha$, with the source weighted norms $|a_{ij}|_\alpha$, $|\delta\widetilde b_i|_\alpha$, and $|\delta^2\widetilde c|_\alpha$ uniformly bounded, where $\delta$ and the weighted norms are defined in the parabolic Hölder convention; (iii) $f$ is parabolic Hölder continuous with $|\delta^2f|_\alpha<\infty$, the initial datum $g$ and lateral datum $\varphi$ are parabolic Hölder continuous, and $g(x)=\varphi(x,0)$ on $\partial U$; (iv) there is $\theta>0$ such that $\theta^2a_{11}+\theta\widetilde b_1\ge1$ on $\Omega$; (v) every spatial boundary point has an exterior tangent ball; and (vi) for constants $\Lambda,v\ge0$,
$$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}(x,t)|^2\le\Lambda,\qquad \lambda_0^{-2}(\|b(x,t)\|^2+\|c(x,t)\|^2)+\lambda_0^{-1}|d(x,t)|\le v^2.$$
For the equation and data conventions in the local parabolic definition, the source asserts that there is a unique classical solution $u^*$.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded, $T>0$, and
$$P[w]=-w_t+\sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}(x,t)D_iD_jw+\sum_{j=1}^d\widetilde b_j(x,t)D_jw+\widetilde c(x,t)w$$

$$\|w\|_{C^0(Q)}\le C_P\left(\|P[w]\|_{C^0(Q)}+\|w\|_{C^0(\Gamma_T)}\right),$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded Lipschitz, $T>0$, and let
$$L_t[e]=\sum_{i,j=1}^dD_i(a_{ij}D_j e+b_i e)+\sum_i c_iD_i e+d e$$
with $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$, $a(x,t)\ge\lambda_0 I$ for some $\lambda_0>0$, and $a,b,c,d$ bounded with the spatial derivatives needed for the displayed divergence form. Fix an input dimension $q\ge1$ and an integer $m\ge0$. Let $\mathcal A_m^{(q)}$ be the class of continuous scalar activations $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ for which there is one depth $n\in\mathbb N$ such that, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, the scalar-output depth-$n$ multilayer perceptrons with activation $\sigma$ are dense in $C^m(K)$ in the $C^m$ norm. For vector outputs, stack scalar-output networks of that same depth. The source notation $\mathcal A_m$ suppresses the input dimension fixed by the finite-dimensional network under consideration. Let $\mathcal A_m^{L,(q)}$ be the subclass whose members are Borel measurable and have at most linear growth, meaning
$$\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}\frac{|\sigma(s)|}{1+|s|}<\infty.$$
For an integer $q\ge1$, define $\mathrm{BA}_q$ to consist of those $\sigma\in\mathcal A_0^{(q)}$ for which, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, every $\varepsilon>0$, and every $C\ge\operatorname{diam}_2(K)$, there is a finite multilayer perceptron $f:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^q$ with
$$|f(x)-x|_2\le\varepsilon\quad(x\in K),\qquad |f(x)|_2\le C\quad(x\in\mathbb R^q).$$
Here $\operatorname{diam}_2(K)=\sup_{x,y\in K}|x-y|_2$. The diameter-based global bound is part of this definition and is retained verbatim; its nonemptiness is checked separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz open set, with $d\ge1$, and let $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Let $X$ be either $W^{m,p}(D;\mathbb R)$ for $1\le p<\infty$, including $W^{0,p}(D)=L^p(D)$, or $C^m(\bar D;\mathbb R)$. In the latter space derivatives in $D$ extend continuously to $\bar D$, and the norm is $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{\bar D}|D^\alpha u|$. For every norm-compact $K\subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a bounded finite-rank linear map $F:X\to X$ such that $\sup_{u\in K}\|Fu-u\|_X<\varepsilon$ and whose range is contained in the restrictions to $D$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, with their continuous boundary values in the $C^m$ case. In particular, such smooth restrictions are norm-dense in $X$.

Moreover, there are finitely many ambient smooth cutoffs $\psi_j$, vectors $v_j$, a unit-mass $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, and $t_0>0$ such that for $0<t<t_0$ the kernel $k_t(x,y)=\sum_j\psi_j(x)\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, with $\rho_t(z)=t^{-d}\rho(z/t)$, defines bounded linear smoothing maps $S_tu(x)=\int_Dk_t(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. They satisfy $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}<\infty$ and $\sup_{u\in K}\|S_tu-u\|_X\to0$ for every norm-compact $K\subset X$. Each kernel is ambient smooth with fixed compact support in its first variable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge1$ and use the finite scalar single-hidden-layer family

$$\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}=\left\{x\mapsto c+\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j):m\in\mathbb N_0,\ c,a_j,b_j\in\mathbb R,\ w_j\in\mathbb R^d\right\}.$$

For every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ is not equal almost everywhere to a polynomial, then $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$. More generally, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ is not polynomial almost everywhere, this family is dense for the essential-supremum seminorm on each such $K$ with respect to $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. If instead $\sigma$ agrees almost everywhere with a polynomial of degree at most $q$ for some $q\in\mathbb N_0$ (including the zero polynomial), the family is not uniformly dense on the segment $\{te_1:0\le t\le1\}$, and is not dense in the Lebesgue essential-supremum seminorm on $[0,1]^d$. Thus pointwise compact-uniform density for $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$, and essential-supremum density for $\mathcal M$, each hold on every compact set if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere.

Let $1<p<\infty$, and let $\mu$ be a finite regular Borel measure concentrated on a compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Form the real $L^p(\mu)$ space using the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, a network is interpreted in this space through any Borel representative agreeing with it outside a Lebesgue-null set; these representatives exist, are integrable on $K$, and give a unique $L^p(\mu)$ class. This convention does not alter the actual pointwise network used in the uniform clause. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ and $\mu(\mathbb R^d)>0$, $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is dense in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere. If $\mu=0$, then $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)=\{0\}$ and the network family is dense for every $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, including polynomial activations.

These are existence statements without a quantitative width bound. They imply neither trainability nor statistical generalization, and compact-uniform approximation does not mean uniform approximation on all of $\mathbb R^d$.
For each $q\ge1$, the class $\mathrm{BA}_q$ in the displayed activation-class definition is empty.

derivations.claim: If $K$ is empty choose the zero operator. Otherwise put $T=G^\dagger|_K$ and choose $0<\tau<\varepsilon/5$. Every listed input space injects continuously into $L^1(D)$: for finite $p$, $\|a\|_1\le |D|^{1-1/p}\|a\|_p\le |D|^{1-1/p}\|a\|_{W^{m,p}}$ when applicable, and for $C(\bar D)$ use $\|a\|_1\le|D|\|a\|_\infty$. Thus each smooth moment $a\mapsto\int_D\varphi a$ is continuous on $A$ and such moments separate distinct members of $K$, using [F4]; distinct continuous functions also differ on an interior set of positive measure.

The corrected property has concrete instances. For ReLU and a compact $S\subset\mathbb R^q$, suppose $C\ge\sup_S|z|_2$. If $S$ is empty choose zero. If $C=0$, then $S\subset\{0\}$ and again choose zero. If $C>0$, the coordinate clamp $c_j(z)=-C+\operatorname{ReLU}(z_j+C)-\operatorname{ReLU}(z_j-C)$ is an exact ReLU network onto $[-C,C]^q$ and fixes $S$. The radial projection $P$ onto the Euclidean ball of radius $C$ is continuous and fixes $S$. By [F6] approximate $P$ on the cube by a ReLU MLP $p$ with Euclidean error $<\xi$, where $0<2\xi<\eta$. Then $b(z)=Cp(c(z))/(C+\xi)$ is a finite ReLU MLP, globally bounded by $C$, and for $z\in S$ its error is less than $\xi+\xi C/(C+\xi)<2\xi<\eta$. Composition of layered MLPs is a layered MLP because consecutive affine maps merge. ReLU also has linear growth and belongs to every relevant $\mathcal A_0$ by [F6]. Thus this corrected branch is nonvacuous.

The set $Q=\{(a,b)\in K^2:\|T(a)-T(b)\|_U\ge\tau\}$ is compact. For each pair in $Q$ a separating moment from step 1.1 remains nonzero on a neighborhood of that pair. A finite subcover supplies moments $\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_J$ such that $E(a)=(\int_D\varphi_ja)_{j=1}^J$ has $E(a)\ne E(b)$ for all $(a,b)\in Q$. If $Q$ is nonempty, the positive continuous function $|E(a)-E(b)|_2$ on $Q$ has a positive minimum $r$; if $Q$ is empty set $J=1$, $\varphi_1=0$, and $r=1$. In both cases $|E(a)-E(b)|_2<r$ implies $\|T(a)-T(b)\|_U<\tau$. This is the complete finite-moment reduction and does not presume a dual representation theorem.

Cover the compact $E(K)$ by finitely many open balls of radius $r/4$ with centers $z_i=E(a_i)$, $a_i\in K$, $1\le i\le s$. Put $h_i(z)=\max(0,r/2-|z-z_i|_2)$, $h_0(z)=\operatorname{dist}(z,E(K))$, and $w_i(z)=h_i(z)/(h_0(z)+\sum_{k=1}^s h_k(z))$. The denominator is positive everywhere: off $E(K)$ its first term is positive, and on $E(K)$ some $h_i>r/4$. Consequently $w=(w_1,\ldots,w_s)$ is continuous on all $\mathbb R^J$, nonnegative, and $\sum_iw_i\le1$, with equality on $E(K)$. For $a\in K$, $w_i(E(a))>0$ implies $|E(a)-E(a_i)|_2<r/2$ and hence $\|T(a)-T(a_i)\|_U<\tau$. The convex combination $\sum_iw_i(E(a))T(a_i)$ therefore differs from $T(a)$ by less than $\tau$.

For every listed output space choose smooth neighborhood restrictions $\phi_i$ with $\|\phi_i-T(a_i)\|_U<\tau$, using [F3]. Define $Bv=\sum_i v_i\phi_i$ and $L=\max(1,\|B\|_{\ell^1\to U})$. Since the weights in step 3.1 sum to one on $E(K)$, $\sup_K\|T(a)-Bw(E(a))\|_U<2\tau$. This is the output finite-dimensional factorization.

Let $Z=\{z:\operatorname{dist}(z,E(K))\le1\}$, a compact subset of $\mathbb R^J$. Uniform continuity of $w$ on $Z$ gives $0<\delta<1$ such that $z,z'\in Z$ and $|z-z'|_2<\delta$ imply $|w(z)-w(z')|_1<\tau/L$. Set $R=\max(1,\sup_{a\in K}\|a\|_1)$. By the $\sigma_2$ premise [F1] choose common-depth scalar networks $p_j$ with $\sup_{\bar D}|p_j-\varphi_j|<\delta/(2R\sqrt J)$. Then $\widetilde E(a)=(\int_Dp_j(y)a(y)\,dy)_j$ satisfies $\sup_K|\widetilde E-E|_2<\delta/2$, so $\widetilde E(K)\subset Z$ and $\sup_K\|Bw(E(a))-Bw(\widetilde E(a))\|_U<\tau$. The input layer kernel $(x,y)\mapsto(p_j(y))_j$ ignores $x$ and has exactly constant spatial output. The estimate uses only $L^1$ bounds and covers $p_1=1$.

Apply the $\sigma_1\in\mathcal A_0$ premise to the continuous map $w$ on compact $\widetilde E(K)$, obtaining a finite MLP $f:\mathbb R^J\to\mathbb R^s$ such that $\sup_{z\in\widetilde E(K)}|f(z)-w(z)|_1<\tau/L$. Then $\sup_K\|Bw(\widetilde E(a))-Bf(\widetilde E(a))\|_U<\tau$. Only $C^0$ approximation of this middle map is used; no differentiability of $\sigma_1$ is needed.

Put $V=\max(1,\sup_{a\in K}|f(\widetilde E(a))|_1)$, finite by continuity and compactness. Define $c_U=1$ for $U=C^{m_2}(\bar D')$ with the maximum derivative norm, and $c_U=(J_{m_2}|D'|)^{1/p_2}$ for $U=W^{m_2,p_2}(D')$ with the usual sum-of-$p_2$-powers norm, where $J_m$ counts multi-indices of order at most $m$; this also treats $L^{p_2}$ with $J_0=1$. For $C^{m_2}$ functions $u$, directly integrating each derivative gives $\|u\|_U\le c_U\|u\|_{C^{m_2}}$. By $\sigma_3\in\mathcal A_{m_2}$ choose common-depth networks $q_i$ such that $\|q_i-\phi_i\|_{C^{m_2}(\bar D')}<\tau/(c_UV)$. These approximants are chosen from the $C^{m_2}$ network subfamily supplied by that density premise, so their derivatives exist. With $\widetilde Bv=\sum_i v_iq_i$, the estimate $\|(\widetilde B-B)v\|_U\le c_U|v|_1\max_i\|q_i-\phi_i\|_{C^{m_2}}$ yields $\sup_K\|\widetilde Bf(\widetilde E(a))-Bf(\widetilde E(a))\|_U<\tau$. Equivalent choices of standard Banach norms merely change $c_U$.

Write the middle MLP as $f(z)=A_{n+1}\sigma_1(A_n\sigma_1(\cdots\sigma_1(A_1z+b_1)\cdots)+b_n)+b_{n+1}$ with $n$ hidden layers. On a spatially constant field $v(y)=z$, the affine map $z\mapsto Az+b$ is represented exactly by the integral kernel $A/|D|$ and constant bias $b$. Such constants are exact $\sigma_2$ networks through their output biases. Use these layers after the input layer of step 5.1, placing precisely the $n$ coordinatewise $\sigma_1$ activations of $f$ between them. The final kernel $\kappa(x,y)=|D|^{-1}(q_1(x),\ldots,q_s(x))$ is a $\sigma_3$ network ignoring $y$, so its integral over $D$ sends a constant $v$ to $\widetilde Bv$. This proves that $G(a)=\widetilde Bf(\widetilde E(a))$ belongs to $\mathrm{NO}_{n+2}$ under the indexing convention in [F2]. All intermediate fields are constant and the final output belongs to $U$ for every $a\in A$.

Adding the four errors in steps 4.1–7.1 gives $\sup_K\|T(a)-G(a)\|_U<5\tau<\varepsilon$. This proves the core theorem. The proof in fact only needs continuity of $T$ on $K$ and the continuous injective $L^1$ realization of $A$; it retains all the listed source spaces.

For the corrected additional branch assume $U$ Hilbert, $M>0$, and $\sup_A\|G^\dagger(a)\|_U\le M$. Apply the core construction with an error $0<\gamma<\min(M,\varepsilon/2)$, calling the resulting operator $G_0$. It has the exact form $G_0(a)=\sum_i f_i(\widetilde E(a))q_i$. Choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_t$ for the finite-dimensional span of the $q_i$, discarding linear dependences, and express $G_0(a)=\sum_jg_j(\widetilde E(a))e_j$. Each $g_j$ is a linear combination of the $f_i$ and hence the same-depth $\sigma_1$ MLP; each $e_j$ is a linear combination of the $q_i$ and hence a same-depth $\sigma_3$ network. If the span is zero the zero operator already suffices. Otherwise $|g(\widetilde E(a))|_2=\|G_0(a)\|_U<M+\gamma<2M$ on $K$.

The set $S=g(\widetilde E(K))$ is compact with radius at most $2M$. Apply the explicitly corrected property in the Statement with $C=2M$ and tolerance $0<\eta<\varepsilon-\gamma$, obtaining $b$. Compose its $\sigma_1$ MLP with $g$ and use final kernel $|D|^{-1}(e_j(x))_j$. By step 8.1 this is an operator $G_1$ of the required architecture. Orthonormality gives $\sup_K\|G_1-G_0\|_U<\eta$ and $\|G_1(a)\|_U=|b(g(\widetilde E(a)))|_2\le2M\le4M$ for every $a\in A$. Thus its approximation error is below $\gamma+\eta<\varepsilon$. The argument handles arbitrary positive $M$ without the source's unjustified normalization $M\ge1$.

For the exact printed additional implication the premise $\sigma_1\in\mathrm{BA}$ is impossible by [F5], so that implication is true but has no instances. Steps 10.1–11.1 establish the explicitly different nonvacuous branch; neither step alters the diameter-based class. This completes all asserted implications.

For the continuous-function architecture, given a finite partition of $D$ into measurable cells $E_1,\dots,E_N$, choose tags $\xi_j\in E_j$ and weights $\omega_j=|E_j|$. For input samples $v_0(\xi_j)$, replace each integral layer by

At an arbitrary output query $x\in\bar D'$, evaluate the same layer formula using $x$ in the first kernel argument and the stored input-cell values in the sum. Apply the pointwise lifting and projection networks with the same parameters at every discretization. A refinement changes the cells, tags, and weights, but not the continuum parameters $W_t,\kappa_t,b_t$ or the pointwise network parameters.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge1$ and use the finite scalar single-hidden-layer family

$$\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}=\left\{x\mapsto c+\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j):m\in\mathbb N_0,\ c,a_j,b_j\in\mathbb R,\ w_j\in\mathbb R^d\right\}.$$

For every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ is not equal almost everywhere to a polynomial, then $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$. More generally, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ is not polynomial almost everywhere, this family is dense for the essential-supremum seminorm on each such $K$ with respect to $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. If instead $\sigma$ agrees almost everywhere with a polynomial of degree at most $q$ for some $q\in\mathbb N_0$ (including the zero polynomial), the family is not uniformly dense on the segment $\{te_1:0\le t\le1\}$, and is not dense in the Lebesgue essential-supremum seminorm on $[0,1]^d$. Thus pointwise compact-uniform density for $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$, and essential-supremum density for $\mathcal M$, each hold on every compact set if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere.

Let $1<p<\infty$, and let $\mu$ be a finite regular Borel measure concentrated on a compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Form the real $L^p(\mu)$ space using the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, a network is interpreted in this space through any Borel representative agreeing with it outside a Lebesgue-null set; these representatives exist, are integrable on $K$, and give a unique $L^p(\mu)$ class. This convention does not alter the actual pointwise network used in the uniform clause. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ and $\mu(\mathbb R^d)>0$, $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is dense in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere. If $\mu=0$, then $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)=\{0\}$ and the network family is dense for every $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, including polynomial activations.

These are existence statements without a quantitative width bound. They imply neither trainability nor statistical generalization, and compact-uniform approximation does not mean uniform approximation on all of $\mathbb R^d$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For integers $n\ge2$ put $t_n=3\cdot2^{-n-2}$, $w_n=2^{-4n-4}$, $H_n=2^{2n}$ and $\rho_n(s)=H_n\beta((s-t_n)/w_n)$. Their supports are disjoint subintervals of $(0,1)$: successive centers differ by $3\cdot2^{-n-3}$, which exceeds $w_n+w_{n+1}$, and each radius is smaller than its center. Define $\rho(s)=\sum_{n\ge2}\rho_n(s)$ for $s>0$, and $\rho(s)=0$ for $s\le0$. On each compact subinterval of $(0,\infty)$ only finitely many summands are nonzero. Moreover $m_n=\int\rho_n\le2H_nw_n=2^{-2n-3}$, so $B=\sum_{n\ge2}m_n<1$. Define $\sigma(s)=\int_0^s\rho(t)\,dt$ for $s\ge0$ and $\sigma(s)=0$ for $s<0$. The tail mass bound proves continuity at zero and uniform convergence of the primitives $\sigma_n(s)=\int_0^s\rho_n(t)\,dt$; thus $\sigma=\sum\sigma_n$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, bounded by $B$, and smooth on $(0,\infty)$. It is a legitimate continuous activation. It is bounded and nonconstant, hence is not polynomial even almost everywhere: continuity would make an almost-everywhere polynomial identity hold everywhere, and a bounded polynomial is constant. Thus [F3] also places it in every finite-dimensional $\mathcal A_0$ class if that premise is imposed when defining the source integral subclass. ReLU belongs to $\mathcal A_0^L$ by the same supplier and its linear growth.

Set $\kappa(x,y)=\sigma(x+y)$ and $G(a)(x)=\int_0^1\sigma(x+y)a(y)\,dy$. The kernel is exactly a one-hidden-unit network on $(x,y)$ with weights $(1,1)$, activation $\sigma$, output weight $1$, and zero biases. The other activations can be the identity. Each $G_n^*(a)(x)=\int_0^1\sigma_n(x+y)a(y)\,dy$ is $C^1$, with derivative $\int_0^1\rho_n(x+y)a(y)\,dy$, and both its function norm and derivative norm are at most $m_n\|a\|_\infty$. Consequently both the function series and derivative series converge uniformly. To verify differentiation without an interchange assumption, the finite partial sums satisfy $S_N(x)-S_N(0)=\int_0^x S_N'(t)\,dt$; uniform convergence permits passage to the limit in this equality, and the fundamental theorem of calculus gives a continuous derivative. Hence $G:A\to U$ is bounded linear, with $\|G(a)\|_U\le2B\|a\|_\infty$. Both $A$ and $U$ embed continuously into $C([0,1])$. To instantiate the source integral subclass as well, take $S_0$ and $S_1$ to have constant kernel $1$ and zero bias, and use $\kappa(x,y)=\sigma(x+y)$ as the final kernel, choosing ReLU for the input and intermediate kernel networks and activations. No intermediate activation occurs at depth $N=2$. This yields $\widehat G(a)=(\int_0^1a)G(1)$, a bounded map $A\to U$. For $a=1$, both preceding integral layers and their quadratures are exactly the constant $1$, so its final continuum and quadrature outputs are precisely those analyzed below. Constant kernels are exact networks through their affine output biases.

At refinement $n$ partition $(0,1)$ into $2^n$ dyadic cells of length $h_n=2^{-n}$. Choose the first tag to be $t_n\in(0,h_n)$ and choose the midpoint of every other cell. Since every tag is positive, each summand is smooth in a neighborhood of $[0,1]$, so $Q_n(a)\in U$. For $a=1$, all derivative summands are nonnegative and $Q_n(1)'(0)\ge h_n\rho(t_n)=h_nH_n=2^n$. Writing its modulus of continuity as $\omega$, the cellwise estimate gives $\|Q_n(1)-G(1)\|_\infty\le\omega(h_n)\to0$. Let $X$ be a Banach space. It has the **approximation property** (AP) if for
every norm-compact set $C\subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a
bounded finite-rank operator $T:X\to X$ such that

$$\sup_{x\in C}\|Tx-x\|<\varepsilon.$$

Here finite rank means that $T(X)$ is finite-dimensional.

For $\lambda\ge0$, $X$ has the **$\lambda$-bounded approximation property**
($\lambda$-BAP) if the same assertion holds with the additional operator-norm
bound $\|T\|\le\lambda$, where the norm is that of [[def-operator-norm]]. It
has the **bounded approximation property** (BAP) if it has $\lambda$-BAP for
some finite $\lambda$.

No sequence of approximating operators is required; this matters in
nonseparable spaces. Plainly $\lambda$-BAP implies AP.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K \in \{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and the complex case by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. Let
$e:n\to X$ be an ordered basis ([[def-linear-basis]]), and write $e_j:=e(j)$.
Give $\mathbb K^n$ its coordinate $\ell^1$ norm

$$\|(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})\|_1:=\sum_{j<n}|a_j|.$$

Define

$$T:\mathbb K^n\to X,\qquad T(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})=\sum_{j<n} a_j e_j.$$

Then $T$ is a topological isomorphism of normed spaces in the sense of
[[def-topological-isomorphism-of-normed-spaces]].

derivations.claim: If $K$ is empty use zero maps. Otherwise consider all pairs $(x,\rho)$ with $x\in K$ and $\rho>0$ such that $\|T(z)-T(x)\|_Y<\varepsilon/4$ whenever $\|z-x\|_X<3\rho$. Continuity ensures that the balls $B(x,\rho)$ from this family cover $K$; take a finite subcover $B(x_i,\rho_i)$. Put $\delta=\min_i\rho_i>0$. For $x\in K$ and $z\in X$ with $\|z-x\|_X<\delta$, select $i$ with $\|x-x_i\|_X<\rho_i$; then both $x,z$ lie within $3\rho_i$ of $x_i$, so $\|T(z)-T(x)\|_Y<\varepsilon/2$. No compact neighborhood of $K$ is asserted or needed.

Apply AP in $X$ to choose bounded finite-rank $P$ with $\sup_K\|Px-x\|_X<\delta$. By step 1.1, $\sup_K\|T(Px)-T(x)\|_Y<\varepsilon/2$. The set $T(P(K))$ is compact; apply AP in $Y$ to obtain bounded finite-rank $Q$ with $\sup_{x\in K}\|QT(Px)-T(Px)\|_Y<\varepsilon/2$. Thus $QT P$ approximates $T$ on $K$ within $\varepsilon$. This makes only two AP selections and does not require a sequence, an infinite union of compact sets, or a choice principle for sequences.

Choose a finite basis $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_J$ of $P(X)$. Its coordinate functionals are bounded by [F2]; hence $Px=\sum_j\ell_j(x)\alpha_j$ with $\ell_j$ bounded on $X$, by composing those functionals with $P$. Write $Rz=\sum_jz_j\alpha_j$, $E(x)=(\ell_j(x))_j$. Choose a finite basis $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_s$ of $Q(Y)$, with bounded coordinate functionals $c_i$, and put $h_i(z)=c_i(QT(Rz))$ and $Bv=\sum_i v_i\beta_i$. Each $h_i$ is continuous on all $\mathbb R^J$, and $BhE=QTP$. For a zero-dimensional range use one zero basis vector and the zero coefficient map instead of an actual basis. These formulas prove the stated factorization and complete the proof.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice for the weak-derivative uniqueness interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$1\le p\le\infty$. For either real or complex scalars, the displayed
$W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ formula from
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] is independent of the representatives
of its Sobolev and derivative classes and defines a norm: it is finite,
absolutely homogeneous, subadditive, and zero exactly on the zero $L^p$ class.
This holds at $p=1$ and $p=\infty$, and when $k=0$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the only class is zero and the formula is zero.

Under the page measure convention, if a finite family of open sets $U_j\subset\mathbb R^n$ covers compact K, there are smooth nonnegative $\chi_j$ with compact support in $U_j$ such that $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a neighborhood of K. These are ambient smooth functions, also when K is only a $C^1$ hypersurface.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ be nonnegative with
$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$.
For $\varepsilon>0$ put $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$
and
$$\Omega_\varepsilon=\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)>\varepsilon\},\qquad\Omega_\varepsilon=\mathbb R^n\ \text{when }\Omega=\mathbb R^n .$$
Then $\rho_\varepsilon*u$ is defined and smooth on $\Omega_\varepsilon$, and
for every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le k$,
$$D^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*u)=\rho_\varepsilon*(D^\alpha u)\qquad\text{on }\Omega_\varepsilon,$$
as pointwise smooth functions for the constructed representatives and as
almost-everywhere classes. Here $D^\alpha u$ is extended by zero off $\Omega$
in the convolution.

Assume countable choice, let $n\ge1$, and use Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$. Translation $\tau_hf(x)=f(x-h)$ is an isometry of complex $L^p$ for $1\le p\le\infty$ and depends norm-continuously on $h$ for $p<\infty$.

For complex $K\in L^1$ and $f\in L^p$, the convolution
$$(K*f)(x)=\int K(y)f(x-y)\,dy$$
exists absolutely a.e., defines a measurable class independent of representatives, and satisfies $\|K*f\|_p\le\|K\|_1\|f\|_p$.

If $K_\varepsilon\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ satisfy
$$\int K_\varepsilon=1,\qquad M:=\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\|K_\varepsilon\|_1<\infty,\qquad \int_{|y|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(y)|\,dy\longrightarrow0\quad(\delta>0),$$
then $K_\varepsilon*f\to f$ in $L^p$ for $p<\infty$, and uniformly for $f\in C_0(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. For fixed $K\in L^1$, $K*f\in C_0$ when $f\in C_0$. These assertions allow complex and sign-changing kernels. In particular $K_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}K(x/\varepsilon)$ is such an approximate identity whenever $K\in L^1$ and $\int K=1$.

If $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)$ has mass one, $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$, and $f$ is complex locally integrable, then $\rho_\varepsilon*f$ is smooth and
$$\partial^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*f)=(\partial^\alpha\rho_\varepsilon)*f.$$
A compactly supported input gives a compactly supported output. No general $L^\infty$ translation-continuity or approximate-identity convergence is asserted.

Let $(X,\mu)$ and $(Y,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces, let
$1 \le p < \infty$, and let $F : X \times Y \to \mathbb{C}$ be measurable with

$$ \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(X)}\,d\nu(y) < \infty. $$

Then the function
$$ H(x) := \int_Y |F(x,y)|\,d\nu(y) $$
belongs to $L^p(X)$ and

$$ \|H\|_{L^p(X)} \le \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(X)}\,d\nu(y). $$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open,
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ have real
and imaginary parts of class $C^k$. For each multi-index
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ with $|\alpha|\le k$, the componentwise classical
derivative $\partial^\alpha u$ is locally integrable and is the weak
derivative $D^\alpha u$. By the uniqueness lemma, it represents the unique
locally integrable weak-derivative class. For $\alpha=0$, this says
$D^0u=u$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion is vacuous: there is only the zero
class and every displayed test identity is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: If $D=\varnothing$, $X$ is the zero space; take $F=0$, the empty cutoff family, $k_t=0$, $S_t=0$ and $t_0=1$. If $K=\varnothing$ the compact approximation clause is vacuous and $F=0$ suffices; the smoothing construction below depends only on $D$ and $X$, and can be obtained by carrying it out with $K=\{0\}$. Henceforth both sets are nonempty. In particular $0<|D|<\infty$, because $D$ contains a ball and is bounded. Fix one boundary chart $Q$, with Lipschitz graph function $\varphi$ of constant $L$, and an ambient neighborhood $U$ of its boundary point with $\bar U\subset Q$ compact. In chart coordinates set $v=(L+2)e_d$. For $x\in\bar D\cap\bar U$, $|z|\le1$, and sufficiently small $t>0$, uniformly in $x,z$, the point $y=x+tv-tz$ stays in $Q$ because $t(|v|+1)<\operatorname{dist}(\bar U,Q^c)$. Moreover $y_d-\varphi(y')\ge x_d-\varphi(x')+t(L+2)-t|z_d|-Lt|z'|\ge t>0$. Thus $\overline B(x+tv,t)\Subset D$. Rotate $v$ back to the original coordinates.

The compact boundary admits finitely many such $U_j$, $1\le j\le J$, covering it. The compact remainder $\bar D\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^JU_j$ lies in $D$; cover it by finitely many balls with closures in $D$, and let $U_0$ be their union, omitting it if the remainder is empty. Then $\bar U_0\Subset D$, so $v_0=0$ has the same ball property for sufficiently small $t$. Apply [F2] to this finite open cover of $\bar D$, obtaining $\psi_j\in C_c^\infty(U_j)$ with $\sum_j\psi_j=1$ near $\bar D$. The minimum of the finitely many positive bounds on $t$ gives $t_0>0$ such that $\overline B(x+tv_j,t)\Subset D$ for every $x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$ and $0<t<t_0$. Taking the family of all admissible chart neighborhoods before extracting a finite subcover avoids selecting a chart independently at every boundary point.

By [F9] choose a nonnegative smooth bump compactly supported in $B_1(0)$ and positive on $\overline B_{1/2}(0)$, and divide it by its positive integral to obtain $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B_1(0))$ with $\int\rho=1$. Put $\rho_t(w)=t^{-d}\rho(w/t)$. Every $u\in X$ belongs continuously to $L^1(D)$: use [F8] for Sobolev spaces, and $\|u\|_1\le |D|\|u\|_{C^m}$ for $C^m$. For its zero extension $E_0u$ define $H_{j,t}u(x)=(\rho_t*E_0u)(x+tv_j)$ and $S_tu=\sum_j\psi_jH_{j,t}u$. By [F4] these are well-defined linear constructions independent of representatives and $S_tu\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$.

First take $X=W^{m,p}(D)$. For every $|\gamma|\le m$ and $x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$, [F3] and step 2.1 give $$D^\gamma H_{j,t}u(x)=\int\rho(z)(E_0D^\gamma u)(x+t(v_j-z))\,dz.$$ The translated center has distance greater than $t$ from $D^c$: the entire closed ball of radius $t$ is a compact subset of $D$. The identity consequently holds on a neighborhood of each indicated $x$. Equivalently the defining weak-derivative identity can be tested against $y\mapsto\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, whose support is compact in $D$; its two derivative signs cancel. Only interior values are used, with no assertion that derivatives commute with zero extension across $\partial D$.

For $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^d)$ define $T_{j,t}f(x)=\int\rho(z)f(x+t(v_j-z))\,dz$ and $\omega_f(r)=\sup_{|h|\le r}\|f(\cdot+h)-f\|_p$. Translation invariance and [F5] give $\|T_{j,t}f\|_p\le\|f\|_p$ and $$\|T_{j,t}f-f\|_p\le\omega_f((|v_j|+1)t).$$ By [F4], $\omega_f(r)\to0$ as $r\downarrow0$. The integral estimates also apply when $p=1$, where [F5] follows directly from Tonelli.

Fix $0<t<t_0$. Write $k_t(x,y)=\sum_j\psi_j(x)\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, so $S_tu(x)=\int_D k_t(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. Fix a closed box $Q$ containing $\bar D$. The finitely many $D_x^\alpha k_t$, $|\alpha|\le m$, are smooth and uniformly continuous on the compact set $\bar D\times Q$ by [F7]. For any $\eta>0$, partition $Q$ into finitely many measurable cells $Q_\ell$ of small enough diameter, assigning shared and outer faces consistently, and choose $y_\ell\in Q_\ell$. Their diameters can be chosen so that $|D_x^\alpha k_t(x,y)-D_x^\alpha k_t(x,y_\ell)|<\eta$ for $x\in\bar D$, $y\in Q_\ell$ and $|\alpha|\le m$. The point $y_\ell$ need not lie in $D$.

Set $f_\gamma=E_0D^\gamma u$. The finite Leibniz rule [F6], step 4.1 and $\sum_j\psi_j=1$ near $\bar D$ give, for $|\alpha|\le m$, the a.e. identity on $D$ $$D^\alpha(S_tu-u)=\sum_j\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\psi_j)\bigl(T_{j,t}f_{\alpha-\beta}-D^{\alpha-\beta}u\bigr).$$ Every derivative $D^\beta\psi_j$ vanishes off $\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$, so step 4.1 supplies exactly the identities used in this formula. All these fixed multiplier derivatives are bounded. Step 4.2 and the finite norm sum [F1] therefore imply $\|S_tu-u\|_{W^{m,p}}\to0$. The same Leibniz formula without subtracting $u$, and $\|T_{j,t}f_\gamma\|_p\le\|f_\gamma\|_p\le\|u\|_{W^{m,p}}$, give $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}\le M_X<\infty$. For example take the $\ell^p$ norm over $\alpha$ of $\sum_{j,\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}\|D^\beta\psi_j\|_\infty$. This argument includes $m=0$ and $p=1$.

Now take $X=C^m(\bar D)$. By [F6] each bounded classical derivative is its weak derivative, so $u\in W^{m,1}(D)$ and step 4.1 applies. Each $D^\gamma u$ is uniformly continuous on $\bar D$ by [F7]. For $x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$, every sampled $y=x+t(v_j-z)$ lies in $D$ and $|y-x|\le(|v_j|+1)t$. Positivity and mass one of $\rho$ thus give $$\sup_{x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j}|D^\gamma H_{j,t}u(x)-D^\gamma u(x)|\le\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\bar D\\|x-y|\le(|v_j|+1)t}}|D^\gamma u(y)-D^\gamma u(x)|\longrightarrow0.$$ The formula of step 5.1, first on $D$ and then by continuity on $\bar D$, gives $\|S_tu-u\|_{C^m}\to0$. Bounding each averaged derivative by $\|D^\gamma u\|_\infty$ and summing the same fixed multiplier constants gives $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}\le M_X<\infty$ also in this case.

Define $$F_{t,\eta}u(x)=\sum_\ell k_t(x,y_\ell)\int_{D\cap Q_\ell}u(y)\,dy.$$ Each coefficient is a bounded linear functional by step 3.1, and there are finitely many coefficients. Each range function $k_t(\cdot,y_\ell)$ belongs to $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, so the operator has finite rank with the required smooth range. Comparison with the integral for $S_t$ gives $$\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{\bar D}|D^\alpha(F_{t,\eta}-S_t)u|\le\eta\|u\|_{L^1(D)}.$$ For $X=C^m(\bar D)$, this yields $\|F_{t,\eta}-S_t\|_{X\to X}\le |D|\eta$. For $X=W^{m,p}(D)$ let $A_m$ be the finite number of multi-indices of order at most $m$. Taking the derivative $L^p$ norms and then applying [F8] gives $\|F_{t,\eta}-S_t\|_{X\to X}\le A_m^{1/p}|D|^{1/p}\eta |D|^{1-1/p}=A_m^{1/p}|D|\eta$. Applying this conclusion to the singleton compact set $K=\{u\}$ proves smooth-restriction density for every $u\in X$. Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz open set, with $d\ge1$, and let $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Let $X$ be either $W^{m,p}(D;\mathbb R)$ for $1\le p<\infty$, including $W^{0,p}(D)=L^p(D)$, or $C^m(\bar D;\mathbb R)$. In the latter space derivatives in $D$ extend continuously to $\bar D$, and the norm is $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{\bar D}|D^\alpha u|$. For every norm-compact $K\subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a bounded finite-rank linear map $F:X\to X$ such that $\sup_{u\in K}\|Fu-u\|_X<\varepsilon$ and whose range is contained in the restrictions to $D$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, with their continuous boundary values in the $C^m$ case. In particular, such smooth restrictions are norm-dense in $X$.

Moreover, there are finitely many ambient smooth cutoffs $\psi_j$, vectors $v_j$, a unit-mass $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, and $t_0>0$ such that for $0<t<t_0$ the kernel $k_t(x,y)=\sum_j\psi_j(x)\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, with $\rho_t(z)=t^{-d}\rho(z/t)$, defines bounded linear smoothing maps $S_tu(x)=\int_Dk_t(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. They satisfy $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}<\infty$ and $\sup_{u\in K}\|S_tu-u\|_X\to0$ for every norm-compact $K\subset X$. Each kernel is ambient smooth with fixed compact support in its first variable.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Under the page measure convention, if a finite family of open sets $U_j\subset\mathbb R^n$ covers compact K, there are smooth nonnegative $\chi_j$ with compact support in $U_j$ such that $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a neighborhood of K. These are ambient smooth functions, also when K is only a $C^1$ hypersurface.

derivations.claim: Empty $K$ or $L=0$ is handled by $\kappa=0$. Otherwise [F1] permits choosing $t>0$ with $\sup_K\|S_ta-a\|_X<\varepsilon/(2\|L\|)$. For fixed $t$, the map $y\mapsto k_t(\cdot,y)|_D$ is ambient $C^\infty$ with values in $X$: every mixed $x$ and $y$ derivative is uniformly continuous on compact products, so the ordinary finite-dimensional Taylor remainders in $y$, uniformly for $x$ derivatives through order $m$, tend to zero in the $C^m$ norm and hence in the $X$ norm. Thus $\kappa_t(y)=L(k_t(\cdot,y)|_D)$ is ambient smooth, with $D_y^\alpha\kappa_t=L(D_y^\alpha k_t(\cdot,y)|_D)$. It is bounded on $\bar D$.

Compactness of $K$ in $X$ implies its compactness in $L^1(D)$ by [F2]. Given $\theta>0$, take a finite $\theta/2$ net $a_1,\ldots,a_s$ in that $L^1$ image. By integrability and an exhaustion of $D$ by compact subsets, there is one compact $F\subset D$ with $\int_{D\setminus F}|a_i|<\theta/2$ for all $i$. Therefore $\sup_{a\in K}\int_{D\setminus F}|a|<\theta$. Choose a smooth cutoff $0\le\zeta\le1$, compactly supported in $D$, equal to one on $F$; use [F3] for the one-set open cover $\{D\}$ of $F$. Then $\sup_K\int_D(1-\zeta)|a|<\theta$. This uses a finite net and finitely many integrable tails, including at $p=1$; it requires no $L^\infty$ approximation of a dual coefficient.

For each $a\in X$, one has $L(S_ta)=\int_D\kappa_t(y)a(y)\,dy$. To justify the identity without assuming a vector-integration theorem, partition a box containing $D$ into cells of diameter tending to zero and replace $k_t(\cdot,y)$ on each cell by $k_t(\cdot,y_l)$. Uniform continuity of every $x$ derivative through order $m$ makes the error in $X$ at most $c_X\eta\|a\|_1$, where $\eta\to0$ is the uniform kernel derivative error and $c_X$ converts a $C^m$ bound to an $X$ bound. Applying bounded $L$ to the finite sums is legitimate by linearity. Their scalar integral errors are at most $\|L\|c_X\eta\|a\|_1$ as well, so passing to the limit proves the identity. Consequently $\sup_K|L(a)-\int_D\kappa_ta|<\varepsilon/2$.

If $\|\kappa_t\|_{L^\infty(D)}=0$, choose $\kappa=0$. Otherwise use step 1.2 with $\theta=\varepsilon/(2\|\kappa_t\|_\infty)$ and set $\kappa=\zeta\kappa_t\in C_c^\infty(D)$. The cutoff error satisfies $\sup_K|\int_D(\kappa_t-\kappa)a|\le\|\kappa_t\|_\infty\sup_K\int_D(1-\zeta)|a|<\varepsilon/2$. Combining with step 2.1 proves the claim.
